questions.q: Why does this lesson describe storage waste as 'quieter' than compute waste?
options: Storage waste doesn't trigger an availability alert or page anyone, so it can go unnoticed for a long time while still billing
Storage costs are always smaller than compute costs in every cloud bill
Cloud providers don't allow storage costs to appear on a cost report
Unattached disks automatically delete themselves after 30 days by default
questions.explain: An unattached disk or old snapshot doesn't show up on an availability dashboard or page an on-call engineer — it just keeps costing money until someone goes looking for it.

questions.q: What do Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management rules and Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules both do?
options: They automatically resize VMs based on CPU utilization
They automatically move or expire data between storage tiers based on age or access pattern, without manual intervention
They automatically delete any object older than 24 hours regardless of configuration
They convert Reserved Instances into Savings Plans automatically
questions.explain: Both act on blob/object age or last-access time to transition data to cooler tiers and eventually expire it, following rules you configure rather than a manual process.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against moving frequently-read application data to a cool or archive storage tier 'to save money'?
options: Archive tiers are always more expensive to store data in than Standard tier
Cool and archive tiers cannot be configured through lifecycle rules at all
Frequently-read data moved to a cheaper, slower tier just shifts the cost onto a retrieval bill, with a latency hit added on top
Lifecycle rules only work on blob storage, never on application data of any kind
questions.explain: Cool/archive tiers trade lower storage cost for slower and sometimes costlier retrieval; routinely-read data moved there just relocates the expense while adding latency.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a classic orphaned-resource candidate in this lesson?
options: A VM scale set currently serving production traffic at p95 CPU above 80%
A Reserved Instance that is actively being used by a running workload
A Savings Plan commitment that still has time remaining on its term
An unattached managed disk or EBS volume left behind after the VM that used it was deleted
questions.explain: An unattached managed disk or EBS volume keeps billing for provisioned capacity even though no VM is reading from or writing to it — the classic orphaned-resource pattern.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as the step between finding a candidate for deletion and actually deleting it?
options: Delete it immediately once a CLI query confirms it's unattached, since any delay risks losing the savings
Tag it for deletion and wait a defined grace period so an unnoticed dependency has time to surface, then confirm retention/compliance requirements don't apply
Convert it to a Reserved Instance before deleting, to recover part of the cost
Nothing — storage deletions are reversible, unlike compute changes, so no extra step is needed
questions.explain: Because deletion is irreversible, the lesson recommends confirming it's truly orphaned, checking retention/compliance requirements, and tagging with a grace period before the real delete runs.
